The Reluctant Innovators
By A. MARTINEZ

The very young woman sat on the edge of the sofa and looked nervous. She carefully studied her fingernails and ran her hands through her hair and picked imaginary lint off the upholstery.

"I have a chance to lead the first renewable energy project in Ravenswood, Nordavia," she said.

The older woman studied the very young woman thoughtfully and then leaned over to her tea service and offered her a cup. "It's nice to have these new solar heating systems now. There was a time when we had to be very careful about energy consumption."

The very young woman was annoyed.

"I don't think I want to go," she blurted. "I don't think I would care to spend three years there."

The older woman took a sip and watched the steam rise from her cup.

"You mean you would miss it here, the people you've known and grown up with, the little familiar things that have made up your life here. You're afraid the glamor would wear off and you would get to hate it in Ravenswood."

The very young woman nodded miserably. "I guess that's it."

"Anything else?"

The very young woman found her fingernails extremely fascinating again and finally said, in a low voice, "Yes, there is."

"Someone special?"

A nod confirmed this.

It was the older woman's turn to look thoughtful. "You know, I'm sure, that psychologists and project managers agree that remote installations should be staffed by partners. That is, of course, as soon as it's practical."

"But that might be a long time!" the very young woman protested.

"It might be—but sometimes it's sooner than you think. And the goal is worth it."

"I suppose so, but—"

The older woman smiled. "Still the reluctant innovators," she said, somewhat to herself.

Ruth Wheeler stared at the computer screen.

Three years at the Keystone Research Station and they didn't want her to come back.

Three years in Keystone, Thandor and they thought she'd be glad to stay for more. Just raise her salary or give her a bonus, the every-person-has-their-price idea. They probably thought she liked it there.

Oh, sure, she loved it. Processed food, recycled water, synthetic vitamins, and filtered air until your insides felt as though they were lined with plastic. Life in a cramped, sterile facility where you could take only twenty steps in any one direction. Their little technological marvel of tomorrow with none of the comforts of home, a charming place where you couldn't take a real shower, couldn't enjoy fresh food, and your circadian rhythms didn't work right.

And for double her salary they thought she'd be glad to stay for another two years. Or maybe three. She should probably be glad she had the opportunity.

The screen started to flash again, demanding an answer.

She typed her reply: "No!"

There was a pause and then the screen flashed once more in a sudden fit of bureaucratic rage. Ruth minimized the window and ignored it. She turned to the sleeping quarters on the other side of the facility.

The flashing hadn't awakened anybody; they were still asleep, making the sounds that people usually make in slumber. Miguel Black, half out of his bunk, was snoring peacefully. Oscar Tran, the poor kid who was due for extended duty, was mumbling to himself. Anil Sullivan, with that look of contentment on his face, looked as if he had just entered his personal paradise. Leo Potter and Matthew Russell were lying perfectly still, their covers not mussed, sleeping very lightly.

Lord, Ruth thought, I'll be happy when I can see some other faces.

"What'd they want?" Anil had one eyelid open and a questioning look on his face.

"They wanted me to stay until the next rotation arrives," Ruth whispered back.

"What did you say?"

She shrugged. "No."

"You kept it short," somebody else whispered. It was Leo, up and sitting on the side of his bunk. "If it had been me, I would have told them just what they could do about it."

The others were awake now, with the exception of Oscar who had his face to the wall and a pillow over his head.

Miguel rubbed his eyes sleepily. "Frustrated, aren't you?"

"Kind of. Who wouldn't be?"

"Well, don't let it throw you. They've never been here at Keystone. They don't know what it's like. All they're trying to do is get a good engineer to stay on the job a while longer."

"All they're trying to do," Ruth said sarcastically. "They've got a fat chance."

"They think you've found a home here," Leo said.

"Why the hell don't you guys shut up until morning?" Oscar was awake, looking bitter. "Some of us still have to stay here, you know. Some of us aren't going back today."

No, Ruth thought, some of us aren't going back. You aren't. And Kai's staying, too. Only Kai isn't ever going back.

Anil jerked his thumb toward Oscar's bunk, held a finger to his lips, and walked noiselessly over to the small electric kettle. It was his day for breakfast duty.

The others started organizing their bunks, getting ready for their last day of work at Keystone. In a few hours they'd be relieved by members of the Third rotation and they'd be on their way back to Westfield, Prandoria.

And that includes me, Ruth thought. I'm going home. I'm finally going home.

She walked silently to the one small window in the facility. It was morning—Thandor's harsh northern morning—and she shivered slightly. The rays of the sun were just striking the far edge of the geothermal field and long shadows shot across the barren landscape. The rest of it was still blanketed in a dark jumble of volcanic rock and jagged formations that would make the Badlands look like paradise.

A hundred meters from the research facility she could make out the small memorial, a simple stone marker with a bronze plaque. You could still see the footprints in the ash where the group had gathered around it. It had been more than twenty months ago, but there was little wind to wear those tracks away. They'd be there for years.

That's what happened to people like Kai Howard, Ruth thought. In remote energy research, one mistake could use up your whole quota of chances.

Anil came back with the coffee. Ruth took a cup, grimaced, and forced herself to swallow the rest of it. It had been freeze-dried so long you could almost taste the packaging.

Leo was warming himself over his cup, looking thoughtful. Miguel and Matthew were getting into their thermal suits, getting ready to go outside. Oscar was still sitting on his bunk, trying to ignore them.

"Think we ought to message the transport hub and see if they've left there yet?" Anil asked.

"I talked to them on the last call," Ruth said. "The relief transport left there eighteen hours ago. They should get here"—she looked at her watch—"in about seven hours."

"Ruth, you know, I've been thinking," Leo said quietly. "You've been here just twice as long as the rest of us. What's the first thing you're going to do once you get back?"

It hit them, then. Miguel and Matthew looked blank for a minute and blindly found equipment cases to sit on. The top halves of their suits were still hanging on hooks. Anil lowered his coffee cup and looked grave. Even Oscar glanced up expectantly.

"I don't know," Ruth said slowly. "I guess I was trying not to think of that. I suppose none of us have. We've been like little kids who have waited so long for a holiday that they just can't believe it when it's finally here."

Anil nodded in agreement. "I haven't been here three years like you have, but I think I know what you mean." He warmed up to it as the idea sank in. "Just what the hell are you going to do?"

"Nothing very spectacular," Ruth said, smiling. "I'm going to rent an apartment overlooking the harbor in Westfield, get some real music playing, and drink wine and listen to it and watch the boats on the water below. Then I think I'll see somebody."

"Who's the somebody?" Leo asked.

Ruth grinned. "Oh, just somebody. What are you going to do, Leo?"

"Well, I'm going to do something practical. First of all, I want to turn over all my data analysis to the government. Then I'm going to write a book about renewable energy innovation and then—why, then, I think I'll get drunk!"

Everybody laughed and Ruth turned to Anil.

"How about you, Anil?"

Anil's expression shifted—something complicated passing across his face before he smoothed it away. "Like Leo, I'll first get rid of my obligations to the project. Then I think I'll go home and see my husband."

They were quiet. "I thought all members of the rotations were supposed to be single," Leo said.

"They are." Anil's voice was carefully neutral. "And I can see their reasons for it."

"So how did you end up here?" Miguel asked.

Anil shrugged, his eyes fixed on his coffee cup. "The Commission was paying well. Very well." He paused, then added quietly, "Marcus understood. He's practical about these things."

Leo whistled low. "Must have been quite a conversation."

"We talked it through," Anil said. His thumb traced the rim of his cup. "He agreed it made sense. Financially."

They laughed. Somebody said: "Play your recording, Ruth. Today's the day for it."

The music player was a small, portable model that Ruth had brought with her when she had arrived with the First rotation. The recording was of traditional folk music from her hometown, and though the file was compressed and the audio quality wasn't perfect, the music was good.

Home Again by Sarah Chen.

They ran through it twice. They were beginning to feel it now, Ruth thought. They were going to go home in a little while and the idea was just starting to sink in.

"You know, Ruth," Leo said, "it won't seem like the same old Keystone without you here. Why, we'll think about this place when we're working on our own projects and it just won't have the same appeal."

"Like they say in the service," Matthew said, "you never had it so good. You found a home here."

The others chimed in and Ruth grinned. Yesterday or a week ago they couldn't have done it. She had been there too long and she had hated it too much.

The party quieted down after a while and Miguel and Matthew finished getting into their suits. They still had a section of the geothermal grid to inspect before they left. Leo was right after them. There was a fault line he wanted to examine and some thermal readings he wished to investigate.

And the time went faster when you kept busy.

Ruth stopped them at the airlock. "Remember to check your suits for tears," she warned. "And check the seals on your oxygen masks."

Leo looked sour. "I've gone out at least five hundred times," he said, "and you check me each time."

"And I'd check you five hundred more," Ruth said. "It takes only one mistake. And watch out for unstable ground. You go through one of those thermal vents and that's it, friend."

Leo sighed. "Ruth, you watch us like a mother hen. You see we check our suits, you settle our arguments, you see that we're not bored and that we stay healthy and happy. I think you'd hold our hands if we got scared. But some day, Ruth old friend, you're gonna find out that your little team can watch out for themselves!"

But he checked his suit for tears and tested the seal of his mask before he left.

Only Anil and Ruth were left in the facility. Anil was at the work table, carefully organizing some soil samples.

"I never knew you were married," Ruth said.

Anil didn't look up. "There wasn't much sense in talking about it. You just get to thinking and wanting—and there's nothing you can do about it. You talk about it and it just makes it worse."

"He let you go without any fuss, huh?"

Anil was quiet for a moment. When he spoke, his voice was flat. "Marcus doesn't make fusses. He's sensible." He sealed a sample container with more force than necessary. "When I showed him the Commission's offer letter, he read it twice. Then he got out a calculator and worked through the numbers. Said it would cover the mortgage, put something away for retirement."

"Sounds like he took it well."

"He took it practically." Anil finally looked up, his expression unreadable. "The night before I left, he cooked my favorite meal. Lamb curry, the way his grandmother made it. We ate on the balcony, watched the sunset over the harbor." He paused. "Neither of us said much."

They were silent for a while. "What do you miss most, Ruth?" Anil asked. "Oh, I know what we said a little while ago, but I mean seriously."

Ruth thought a minute. "I think I miss the ocean," she said quietly. "The blue water and the green parks and trees with birds in them. I think, when I go back, that I'd like to go to the beach and just feel the sand between my toes."

She stopped, feeling embarrassed. Anil's expression was encouraging. "And then I think I'd like to go downtown and just watch the shoppers on the sidewalks. Or maybe go to a concert hall and smell the old wood and the people's perfume and cologne."

She studied her hands. "I think what I miss most is people—all kinds of people. Rich people and poor people and tall people and short people, and people I can't understand. People who wouldn't know renewable energy from a toaster. And people who wouldn't give a damn. We're hundreds of miles from civilization, Anil, and to make it poetic, I think I miss my fellow humans more than anything."

"Got someone special back home?" Anil asked almost casually.

"Yes."

"You're not like Oscar. You've never mentioned it."

"Same reason you didn't mention your husband. You get to thinking about it."

Anil sealed the sample container. "Going to get married when you get back?"

Ruth was at the window again, staring out at the bleak landscape. "We hope to."

"Settle down in a nice place and maybe start a family, eh?"

Ruth nodded.

"That's the only future," Anil said. His voice had a strange edge to it.

He put away the container and came over to the window. Ruth moved over so they both could look out. Anil reached into his pocket and pulled out a worn photograph. Marcus, smiling, standing on what looked like a pier with fishing boats behind him.

"He sends me one message a month," Anil said. "Always cheerful. Always practical. Tells me about his work, the garden, the neighbors." He studied the photograph. "Never once asked me to come home early. Never once said—" He stopped, tucked the photo away.

"Said what?"

Anil's jaw tightened. "It's a good opportunity. That's what everyone says. A chance to advance the field, make a real contribution. And the money—" He laughed, but it came out hollow. "The money is excellent. Couldn't have turned it down. Would have been foolish."

"Ruth." Anil hesitated a moment. "What happened to Kai?"

"She died," Ruth said. "She was a brilliant engineer, all wrapped up in the work. Being at Keystone was the opportunity of a lifetime. She thought so much about it that she forgot a lot of little things—like how to stay alive. The day before the Second rotation came, she went out to finish some work she was interested in. She forgot to check for suit tears and whether or not her oxygen mask was properly sealed. We couldn't get to her in time."

"She had her radio with her?"

"Yes. It worked fine, too. We heard everything that went through her mind at the end."

Anil's face was blank. "What's your real job here, Ruth? Why does somebody have to stay for extended duty?"

"Hell, lots of reasons, Anil. You can't get a whole relief crew and let them take over cold. They have to know where you left off. They have to know where things are, how things work, what to watch out for. And then, because you've been here two years and know the ropes, you have to watch them to see that they stay alive in spite of themselves. Keystone's a harsh environment and you have to learn how to live in it. There's a lot of things to learn—and some people just never learn."

"You're a supervisor, then."

"I suppose you could call it that."

Anil said, "You're not a scientist, are you?"

"No, you should know that. I came as the chief engineer of the first installation. We built the facility from prefabricated parts so there wasn't anything to go back on immediately. I'm a good mechanic and I made myself useful with the equipment. When it occurred to us that somebody was going to have to stay for extended duty, I volunteered. I thought the others were so important that it was better they should take their research and data back to Westfield when the first relief transport came."

"You wouldn't do it again, though, would you?"

"No, I wouldn't."

"Do you think Oscar will do as good a job as you've done here?"

Ruth frowned. "Frankly, I hadn't thought of that. I don't believe I care. I've put in my time; it's somebody else's turn now. He volunteered for it. I think I was fair in explaining all about the job when you talked it over among yourselves."

"You did, but I don't think Oscar's the man for it. He's too young, too inexperienced. He volunteered because he thought it made him look like a hero. He doesn't have the judgment that an older person would have. That you have."

Ruth turned slowly around and faced Anil.

"I'm not the indispensable person," she said slowly, "and even if I was, it wouldn't make any difference to me. I'm sorry if Oscar is young. So was I. I've lost three years up here. And I don't intend to lose any more."

Anil held up his hands. "Look, Ruth, I didn't mean you should stay. I know how much you hate it and the time you put in up here. It's just—" His voice trailed away. "It's just that I think it's such a damn important job."

Anil had gone out in a last search for thermal anomalies and Ruth enjoyed one of her relatively few moments of privacy. She wandered over to her bunk and opened her duffel bag. She checked the clothes and her toiletries for maybe the hundredth time and pushed everything down farther in the canvas. It was foolish because the bag was already packed and had been for a week. She remembered putting it off for as long as she could and then the quiet satisfaction about a week before, when she had opened her small locker and transferred its meager belongings to the bag.

She hadn't actually needed to pack, of course. In less than twenty-four hours she'd be back in Westfield where she could buy whatever she wanted. She could leave behind her worn shirts and socks and the oversized jacket she had inherited from—who was it? Martinez?—of the First rotation. Oscar could probably use them or maybe one of the team in the Third.

But it wasn't like going home unless you packed. It was part of the ritual, like marking off the last three weeks in marker on the white wall beside her bunk. Just a few hours ago, when she woke up, she had made the last check mark and signed her name and the date. Her signature was right beneath Kai's.

She frowned when she thought of Kai and zipped up the bag. They should never have sent someone as focused as Kai to Keystone.

She had just secured the bag when she heard the hiss of the airlock and the soft whoosh of air. Somebody had come back earlier than expected. She watched the inner door swing open and the suited figure clump in and remove its helmet.

Oscar. He had gone out to help Miguel on the thermal scanner. Maybe Miguel hadn't needed any help, with Matthew along. Or more likely, considering the circumstances, Oscar wasn't much good at helping anybody today.

Oscar stripped off his suit. His face was covered with light beads of sweat and his eyes were frightened.

He moistened his lips slightly. "Do—do you think they'll ever have relief transports up here more often than every two years, Ruth? I mean, considering the advance of—"

"No," Ruth interrupted bluntly. "I don't. Not at least for ten years. The logistics are too expensive and the conditions too hazardous. On transport costs alone you're worth a fortune when they send you here. Even if it becomes cheaper, Oscar, it won't come about so it will shorten extended duty right away." She stopped, feeling a little sorry for Oscar. "It won't be too bad. There'll be new people up here and you'll pass a lot of time getting to know them."

"Well, you see," Oscar started, "that's why I came back early. I wanted to see you about extended duty. It's that—well, I'll put it this way." He seemed to be groping for an easy way to say what he wanted to. "I'm engaged back home. Really wonderful person, Ruth, you'd like them if you knew them." He fumbled in his pocket and found a photograph and put it on the desk. "That's a picture of Sam, taken at a festival we attended together." Ruth didn't look. "They—we—expected to be married when I got back. I never told them about extended duty, Ruth. They think I'll be home tomorrow. I kept thinking, hoping, that maybe somehow—"

He was fumbling it badly, Ruth thought.

"You wanted to trade places with me, didn't you, Oscar? You thought I might stay for extended duty again, in your place?"

It hurt to look in Oscar's eyes. They were the eyes of a person who was trying desperately to stop what they were about to do, but just couldn't help themselves.

"Well, yes, more or less. Oh, God, Ruth, I know you want to go home! But I couldn't ask any of the others; you were the only one who could, the only one who was qualified!"

Oscar looked as though he was going to be sick. Ruth tried to recall all she knew about him. Oscar Tran. Good at systems thinking. Graduate from one of the top technical schools. Parents were entrepreneurs in the renewable energy sector.

It still didn't add up, not quite. "You know I don't like it here any more than you do," Ruth said slowly. "I may have commitments at home, too. What made you think I would change my mind?"

Oscar took the plunge. "Well, you see," he started eagerly, too far gone to remember such a thing as pride, "you know my parents are pretty well off. We would make it worth your while, Ruth." He was feverish. "It would mean two more years, Ruth, but they'd be well-paid years!"

Ruth felt tired. The good feeling she had about going home was slowly evaporating.

"If you have any report to make, I think you had better get at it," she cut in, keeping all the harshness she felt out of her voice. "It'll be too late after the relief transport leaves. It'll be easier to give the captain your report than try to transmit it back to Westfield from here."

She felt sorrier for Oscar than she could ever remember having felt for anybody. Long after going home, Oscar would remember this.

It would eat at him like a cancer.

Cowardice is the one thing for which no person ever forgives themselves.

Leo was eating a protein bar and looking out the window, so, naturally, he saw the transport first. "Well, look at that!" he shouted. "We got company!" He dashed for his suit. Miguel and Matthew piled after him and all three started for the airlock.

Ruth was standing in front of it. "Check your suits," she said softly. "Just be sure to check."

"Oh, come on, Ruth!" Leo started angrily. Then he shut up and went over his suit. He got to his oxygen mask and turned white. The seal was cracked. It was only half a kilometer to the relief transport, so somebody would probably have got to him in time, but.... He bit his lips and got a replacement.

Ruth and Anil watched them dash across the volcanic landscape, making the careful but quick movements they had all learned. The hatch of the transport had opened and figures were climbing down the ladder. The small figures from the facility reached them and did a short celebration. Then the figures linked arms and started back. Ruth noticed one—it was probably Leo—pat the transport affectionately before he started back.

"Two years," Anil said quietly, watching the figures approach. "Two years of monthly messages. Of being practical."

Ruth glanced at him. His face was composed, but his hands gripped the window frame.

"The Commission pays well," he said, almost to himself. "That's what I told him. That's what I kept telling myself."

They were in the airlock and the air pumped in and then they were in the facility, taking off their suits. The newcomers were impressed and solemn, very much aware of the tremendous responsibility that rested on their shoulders. Like Leo and Anil and the members of the Second rotation had been when they had arrived. Like Ruth had been in the First.

Leo and the others were all over them.

How was it back in Westfield? Who had won the elections? Was so-and-so still teaching at the university? What was the political situation?

Was the sky still blue, was the water still clean, did the leaves still turn color in the autumn, did people still love and cry and were there still people who didn't know what renewable energy was and didn't give a damn?

Ruth had gone through it all before. But was Jamie still Jamie?

Some of the people in the Third had their luggage with them. One of them—a sturdy, dark-haired woman named Sasha Lowe—was opening a box about a foot square and six inches deep. Ruth watched her curiously.

"Well, I'll be damned!" Anil said. "Hey, everyone, look what we've got here!"

Ruth and the others crowded around and suddenly Leo leaned over and took a deep breath. In the box, covering a thick layer of soil, was a small herb garden. They looked at it, awed. Anil put out his hand and touched one of the leaves.

"I like the feel of it," he said simply.

Ruth plucked a single leaf with her fingernail and put it between her lips. It had been years since she had seen fresh herbs and had the luxury of cooking with them and smelling them in a real kitchen.

Sasha blushed. "I thought we could spare a little water for it and maybe use the grow lights on it some of the time. Couldn't help but bring it along; it seemed sort of like a symbol...." She looked embarrassed.

Ruth sympathized. If she had had any sense, she'd have tried to bring something like that up to Keystone instead of her music player.

"That's valuable cargo," Oscar said sharply. "Do you realize that at current transport rates, those herbs are worth about fifty credits a leaf?"

Sasha looked stricken and somebody said, "Oh, shut up, Oscar."

One of the people separated from the group and came over to Ruth. She held out her hand and said, "My name's Chen. Captain of the relief transport. I understand you're in charge here?"

Ruth nodded and shook hands. They hadn't had a captain on the First transport. Just a pilot and crew. Chen looked every inch a captain, too. Strong face, silver-streaked hair, the confident bearing of someone who was sure of herself.

"You might say I'm in charge here," Ruth said.

"Well, look, Ms. Wheeler, is there any place where we can talk together privately?"

They walked over to one corner of the facility. "This is about as private as we can get, captain," Ruth said. "What's on your mind?"

Chen found an equipment case and made herself comfortable. She looked at Ruth.

"I've always wanted to meet the person who's spent more time here than anybody else," she began.

"I'm sure you wanted to see me for more reasons than just curiosity."

Chen took out a pack of mints. "Mind if I have one?"

Ruth jerked a thumb toward Oscar. "Ask him. He's in charge now."

The captain didn't bother. She put the pack away. "You know we have big plans for the station," she said.

"I hadn't heard of them."

"Oh, yes, big plans. They're working on autonomous vehicles now that could carry cargo and materials for more facilities like this. Enable us to enlarge the complex, have a series of buildings all linked together. Make good laboratories and living quarters for you people." Her eyes swept the room. "Have a little privacy for a change."

Ruth nodded. "They could use a little privacy up here."

The captain noticed the pronoun. "Well, that's one of the reasons why I wanted to talk to you, Wheeler. The Commission talked it over and they'd like to see you stay. They feel if they're going to enlarge it, add more facilities and have more people up here, that a person of practical experience should be running things. They figure that you're the only one who's capable and who's had the experience."

The captain vaguely felt the approach was all wrong.

"Is that all?"

Chen was ill at ease. "Naturally you'd be paid well. I don't imagine anyone would like being here all the time. They're prepared to double your salary—maybe even a bonus in addition—and let you have full authority. You'd be Director of the Keystone Energy Research Complex."

All this and a title too, Ruth thought.

"That's it?" Ruth asked.

Chen frowned. "Well, the Commission said they'd be willing to consider anything else you had in mind, if it was more money or...."

"The answer is no," Ruth said. "I'm not interested in more money for staying because I'm not interested in staying. Money can't buy it, captain. I'm sorry, but I'm afraid that you'd have to stay up here to appreciate that.

"Oscar Tran is staying for extended duty. If there's something important about the project or impending changes, perhaps you'd better tell him before you go."

She walked away.

Near the window, Anil stood alone, holding the worn photograph. His thumb traced Marcus's face. From across the room, Ruth could see his lips moving silently—whether in prayer or calculation, she couldn't tell.
problem_data.question: How did Anil feel about leaving his husband to go to Keystone?
problem_data.correct_answer: He regretted it but needed the money the Commission was paying.
problem_data.incorrect_answer: He was excited about the opportunity and his husband fully supported his decision.
answers: He regretted it but needed the money the Commission was paying.
